subtopic: Bystander effect and diffusion of responsibility
passage:
In the student bar in Dublin, three lads from Bilal's course started joking about Rania's headscarf, loud enough for her table to hear. “Is it hiding a bad hair day?” one said. Others laughed.
Bilal sat right there. He stared at his drink. He told himself it wasn't his fight.
Rania gathered her things and left without a word.
Bilal didn't sleep well. By morning the feeling was clear: it was shame, and hiding from it would make it worse.
He found Rania outside the library. “I was there last night. I should have said something. I'm sorry.” She looked at him for a long moment. “Thanks for saying it.”
He wrote one line in his notes app: Next time, say “Not funny, lads,” and sit with her.

qa.q: Where did the joking happen?
qa.a: It happened in the student bar in Dublin.

qa.q: What was Bilal feeling the next morning?
qa.a: He felt ashamed and regretful, and knew that hiding from the feeling would make it worse.

qa.q: Is Bilal's plan for next time a good one, and why?
qa.a: Yes; a short line like "Not funny, lads" and sitting with Rania is simple and safe, so he's more likely to actually do it.

qa.q: How might Rania have felt when Bilal apologised?
qa.a: She seemed cautious but touched; after being mocked while people watched, an honest apology may have eased some of the hurt.

grounding: Shows a young man who watched a classmate being mocked and did nothing, then uses his shame to apologise and plan how to act next time.

At the hostel mess on Saturday night, three seniors made Naveen stand on a bench and sing while they threw bread at him. Forty students watched. Nazia was one of them. She kept eating, eyes down.
All night she saw his face.
On Sunday morning she knocked on the first-years' room. “Naveen, I was in the mess. I didn't do anything. I'm really sorry.”
He shrugged, but his eyes were red.
“Will you come with me to the warden? I'll tell her what I saw.”
They went together. The warden listened to both, thanked Nazia, called the anti-ragging cell that morning and moved the three seniors to another floor while it was looked into.
Nazia told herself: never again with my eyes down.

qa.q: How many students watched in the mess?
qa.a: Forty students watched.

qa.q: How did Nazia feel through the night?
qa.a: She felt guilty and ashamed, unable to stop seeing Naveen's face.

qa.q: What did Nazia do with her guilt, and why was it helpful?
qa.a: She apologised to Naveen and went with him to the warden as a witness, turning regret into action that got the seniors dealt with.

qa.q: How might Naveen have felt when Nazia apologised?
qa.a: He seemed hurt and wary, his eyes red, but may have felt less alone knowing someone would stand with him.

grounding: Shows a young woman who watched a junior being humiliated and did nothing, then apologises and acts as a witness next morning.

passage:
I'm Disha. I was coming up the metro stairs at Rajiv Chowk that evening when I saw him: an older man in a grey sweater, sitting down suddenly against the wall, then sliding sideways.
People kept walking. Dozens. A man stepped over his bag. I slowed down, and I remember thinking, if it were serious, surely someone would stop. Everyone looked so calm.
Then a woman in office clothes, Alka, her ID card said, knelt beside him. “Uncle? Uncle, can you hear me?” She looked up and caught my eye. “Can you get the station staff?”
I ran. The staff came with a wheelchair and called an ambulance.
Afterwards I stood there shaking, thinking how close I came to walking past because nobody else stopped.

qa.q: Where did the man sit down suddenly?
qa.a: Against the wall on the metro stairs at Rajiv Chowk.

qa.q: What was Disha thinking before Alka knelt?
qa.a: Disha felt unsure and read the crowd's calm as a sign it wasn't serious, since surely someone would stop if it were.

qa.q: What worked once Alka stepped in?
qa.a: Alka checked on the man and asked Disha directly to get station staff, which turned a watcher into a helper.

qa.q: How might the man have been affected by the crowd walking past?
qa.a: He was left alone at a dangerous moment, since each person took the others' walking as proof he was fine.

grounding: A commuter recalls seeing a man collapse while the crowd walked on, reading their inaction as proof it wasn't serious, until one person acted.

Wednesday: He saw her again on the same platform, alone, glancing over her shoulder. The same man was near the stairs. Vijay's chest tightened. He walked over and stood beside her. “Everything okay? Want me to walk you to the ladies' coach?”
Dolma let out a long breath. “Yes. Please.” The man turned away. Vijay pointed him out to the railway police constable at the gate, who went after him.
Friday: Vijay kept thinking about Monday, and how the crowd's calm had fooled him.

Noor, you asked why I always stop when someone falls on the road. Let me tell you. I'm your Nilesh chacha, and this is from Delhi, when I was twenty-five.
It was a hot afternoon at the ITO bus stop. A man in a safari suit went down, just folded onto the footpath. Maybe forty of us were there.
And you know what I did? I looked at everyone else. Nobody moved, so I thought, must be nothing, maybe he's drunk. Everybody was thinking the same thing, looking at each other.
Then a college girl screamed, “Why is nobody helping?” It broke the spell. Five of us rushed at once. Someone called an ambulance.
He lived. But I never forgot how forty calm faces almost fooled me.

qa.q: How might the college girl have felt before she screamed?
qa.a: She was probably alarmed and frustrated, seeing a man collapse while forty adults just stood there.

grounding: An elder recalls a man collapsing at a bus stop and a crowd, himself included, reading each other's inaction as proof it wasn't serious.

passage:
At the temple fair in the hill town of Palampur, a man carrying sacks of rice suddenly swayed and dropped beside the jalebi stall. A circle of people formed. Everyone stared. Someone said, “Call someone.” Nobody did.
Amandeep, visiting with her cousins, pushed to the front. She pointed at a boy in a blue shirt. “You. Call the ambulance, 108. Now.” She turned to a woman in a maroon shawl. “Dolma ji, please bring water from your stall.” She pointed at two men. “You two, move the crowd back, give him air.”
The boy was already dialling. Dolma came running with a steel jug. The men waved people back.
The ambulance came up the winding road twenty minutes later. The man was sitting up by then, sipping water.

qa.q: Where did the man drop?
qa.a: He dropped beside the jalebi stall.

qa.q: What was Amandeep feeling as she pushed to the front?
qa.a: She seemed alarmed but determined, frustrated that everyone stared and said "call someone" without doing it.

qa.q: What would you advise others to learn from Amandeep's approach?
qa.a: In an emergency, point at a specific person and give a specific task, because "call someone" leaves everyone waiting.

qa.q: How might the boy in the blue shirt have felt when Amandeep pointed at him?
qa.a: He was probably startled but relieved to have a clear job, and started dialling at once.

grounding: Shows a young woman in an emergency pointing at specific people for specific tasks, breaking the crowd's waiting.

subtopic: Bystander effect and diffusion of responsibility
passage:
On a packed tro-tro in Accra, an old man near the back slumped against the window, his face grey. Passengers murmured. One woman fanned him with a newspaper. Nobody else moved.
Nkechi was standing by the door. She raised her voice over the engine. “Driver! Stop the bus. Please pull over.” Then she pointed. “Kwame, you're by the window, call an ambulance. You, madam with the fan, keep going. You, sir, give him your seat by the door, let's lay him down.”
Kwame fumbled for his phone and dialled. The bus pulled over. Two passengers helped lower the man onto the seat.
Ten minutes later a siren came through the traffic. As the paramedics climbed in, the man squeezed Nkechi's hand.

qa.a: It was in Accra.

qa.q: Why did pointing at people work better than a general shout?
qa.a: Naming Kwame and the others gave each a clear job, so nobody could leave it to someone else.

qa.q: How might the old man have felt when he squeezed Nkechi's hand?
qa.a: He likely felt frightened but grateful and relieved that someone had taken charge.

grounding: Shows a young woman on a bus pointing at specific passengers to call an ambulance and help, breaking the crowd's hesitation.

The college fest decoration team had forty people and one power point that kept tripping. Rain dripped through the canteen roof where they worked.
Tenzin tied a few marigold strings, then sat scrolling his phone. Nobody could tell who did what anyway. Irfan, the coordinator, was shouting at twenty people at once.
Late in the evening, Irfan said, “Tenzin, you take the entrance arch. Just you. Your name goes on the credits board.”
Tenzin looked up. Suddenly the arch was his, and everyone would walk under it. He worked till the guard locked the gate, balancing on a ladder in the rain, fixing each flower himself.
The next day, three people stopped to photograph his arch. He pretended not to watch.

qa.a: He gave him the entrance arch.

qa.a: He felt motivated and responsible, and later quietly proud when people photographed it.

qa.a: Give people specific visible parts with their names on them, so effort doesn't get lost in a crowd.

qa.q: How might Irfan feel seeing Tenzin work till the gate closed?
qa.a: Irfan was probably surprised and relieved that giving one clear job changed Tenzin's effort so much.

grounding: Shows a student whose effort drops in a huge, chaotic team, but who works hard once his part is visible and named.
